The Infamies of the Batiniyya, p. 53. Despite his standing as a scholar, al-Ghazali could not free himself from the outlook of his class. He lived in comfort and luxury, a favourite of the Seljuk sultans' courts and the palaces of their ministers. His close ties to the Seljuk minister Nizam al-Mulk are too well known to need explanation. When he looks down on ordinary people and calls them ignorant, he is therefore expressing the contempt of a privileged class more than he is simply saying that these people lack knowledge, as one might at first suppose. We find much the same thing in a later age when al-Jabarti looks down on ordinary people and calls them the “rabble” (harafish), distinguishing them from the prosperous class of the “children of respectable families”. This clearly reveals the general link between traditionalist thinking and political power, and the affinity of reasoned thought with social justice. ↩

On this subject, see the chapter that De Boer wrote on the Brethren of Purity in his History of Islamic Philosophy, as well as Dr Jabbur Abd al-Nur's book The Brethren of Purity. This community emerged in the second half of the fourth century AH as an underground circle of thinkers based in Basra, with branches in many Iraqi towns. Its appearance as an intellectual movement that sought to spread enlightened thinking and make the “Brethren” aware of the evils of the Abbasid system was a natural consequence of the failure of the revolutionary movements, which the caliphate had met with violence and brutality. Its concentration on the towns of Iraq shows how impossible it was to pursue the path of revolution, which had succeeded only in the outlying regions. After the fall of the Iraqi Qarmatians in 316 AH, the Brethren of Purity gave the movement a new intellectual direction, relying on the word rather than the sword. They produced a series of essays on astronomy, mathematics, geography, music, ethics and philosophy, and circulated them within their community to prepare its members intellectually as a revolutionary vanguard opposed to those in power. In a recent study of the Brethren of Purity, we confirmed these views and discovered that the community dated back to the middle of the third century AH. ↩

Religious ideas were essential to the success of social revolutions in this period. Purely rationalist movements met with no success, and their pioneers were branded apostates and heretics. This explains why the Mu'tazilites were unable to draw the discontented masses to their cause, despite the fact that their beliefs combined reasoned thinking with social justice. Social revolutions with no religious foundation also failed, such as the peasants' revolt led by al-Mubarqa al-Yamani in the reign of al-Mu'tasim in 227 AH, and the Zanj revolt in the middle of the third century AH, despite the successes the latter achieved. Here is the text of the pledge. The advocate says to the person who has responded to the movement:

You bind yourself by God's covenant and pledge, by the protection of His Messenger (peace be upon him), and by the covenant and pledge that God took from the prophets. You will keep secret what you have heard and will hear from me, what you have learned of my affairs and the affairs of the man residing in this town for the rightful leader, the imam, the Mahdi; the affairs of his brothers, companions, children and household; the affairs of those who obey him in this faith; and the sincere followers of the Mahdi and his Shia, men and women, young and old. You will reveal nothing of it, great or small, by which anyone might learn of it, except what I permit you to speak of, or what the person in charge in this town or elsewhere permits you to reveal. In that case you will act within the limits we set for you and will not exceed them. You bind yourself to fulfil what I have set out for you and undertake by God's covenant and pledge to protect me and everyone I name and identify to you from whatever you would protect yourself against. You will be sincerely loyal to us and to the imam for God's sake, openly and in your heart. You will betray neither God, nor His friend, nor any of his helpers and allies, nor anyone connected with him and with us through kinship, wealth or favour. You may not invoke any opinion or other pledge to annul this covenant. If you do any of these things knowing that you have broken it, then you are cut off from God and His messengers, the first and the last, from the angels nearest to Him, and from all the scriptures He revealed to His earlier prophets. You are outside every faith, outside the party of God and within the party of Satan and his allies. May God utterly forsake you and hasten vengeance and punishment upon you if you break anything I have made you swear to, by twisting its meaning or otherwise. If you break any of it, you must make thirty pilgrimages to His House, as a binding vow, walking barefoot. And if you break it, everything you own at the time of your breach is to be given in charity to the poor and needy who are not related to you; every enslaved person you own on that day is to be freed; and every woman who is your wife or whom you marry in future is to be divorced three times if you break any of this. If you intend or conceal in your heart anything contrary to what I mean by this oath, the oath nevertheless binds you from beginning to end. God bears witness to the truth of your intention and the resolve of your conscience. God is sufficient as a witness between me and you. Say: yes. Then the person who has responded says: yes.
